reply: You've reached the goal topic: multiplication rule and probability trees. A tree draws an experiment in stages, with branches at each stage, and every complete path from the root to a tip is one outcome of the whole experiment. The rule that runs the tree is this: a path probability is the product of its conditional branch probabilities. You move along one path, multiply the probability of each branch you take, and the product is the chance of that whole path. Two things follow. You never multiply across different paths, only along one. And when every branch at every stage is equally likely, every complete path is equally likely too, so counting paths works just like counting outcomes. The next problem gives you path counts; your job is to compare favorable paths with all paths.

reply: You can do this; the tree is just a picture, and the picture has only two rules. First, a tree shows an experiment in stages. From the root, branches fan out for the first stage; from each of those, branches fan out for the next stage; and so on until the tips. A complete path runs from the root to one tip, and it stands for one outcome of the whole experiment. Second, a path probability is the product of its conditional branch probabilities: to find the chance of a single path, you multiply the probabilities of the branches along that path, and only that path. You never combine branches from two different paths, because two different paths cannot both happen. When every branch at a stage is equally likely, every complete path ends up equally likely, and then the probability of an event is simply the number of favorable paths over the number of all paths. The problem you have gives you exactly those two numbers. Next time we look at it, we'll just identify which number is which.
